blocks.body:
A problem in the Chinese text Sunzi Suanjing (written some time between the 3rd and 5th centuries) asks for a number of objects which leaves remainder $2$ when counted in threes, remainder $3$ when counted in fives, and remainder $2$ when counted in sevens. The answer given is $23$.

Why is there an answer at all, and how many are there? The Chinese remainder theorem says that if the moduli are pairwise coprime, a system of such conditions always has a solution, and the solution is unique modulo the product of the moduli. Behind this is a structural fact: computing modulo $mn$ is the same as computing modulo $m$ and modulo $n$ side by side.

blocks.title: Sieving by hand
blocks.body:
Start with the first two conditions. The numbers $\equiv 2 \pmod 3$ are $2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, \dots$. Among these, the ones $\equiv 3 \pmod 5$ are $8, 23, 38, 53, \dots$, which go up in steps of $15$: once you have one, adding $15 = 3 \cdot 5$ preserves both conditions, and nothing smaller does. Among $8, 23, 38, \dots$ we want remainder $2$ modulo $7$; the remainders are $1, 2, \dots$, so $23$ works, and the full solution set is $23 + 105k$.

Two things made this work. In each block of $15$ consecutive integers exactly one satisfies the first two conditions, and in each block of $105$ exactly one satisfies all three. The theorem says this always happens when the moduli share no common factors.

blocks.title: Chinese remainder theorem
blocks.body:
Let $m_1, m_2, \dots, m_k$ be pairwise coprime positive integers and $M = m_1 m_2 \cdots m_k$. For any integers $a_1, \dots, a_k$ the system
$$x \equiv a_1 \pmod{m_1}, \quad x \equiv a_2 \pmod{m_2}, \quad \dots, \quad x \equiv a_k \pmod{m_k}$$
has a solution, and any two solutions are congruent modulo $M$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We use two facts from [[bezout]]. First, if $u$ and $v$ are both coprime to $m$, so is $uv$: from $ux + my = 1$ and $vx' + my' = 1$, multiplying gives $uv(xx') + m(\dots) = 1$. By induction a product of numbers coprime to $m$ is coprime to $m$. Second, if $\gcd(m, m') = 1$ and both divide $z$, then $mm' \mid z$.

Existence. For each $i$ let $M_i = M / m_i$, the product of the other moduli. Each of those is coprime to $m_i$, so $\gcd(M_i, m_i) = 1$ and $M_i$ has an inverse $y_i$ modulo $m_i$ ([[mod-inverse]]). Put
$$x = a_1 M_1 y_1 + a_2 M_2 y_2 + \cdots + a_k M_k y_k.$$
Modulo $m_j$, every term with $i \neq j$ vanishes, because $m_j \mid M_i$. The remaining term is $a_j M_j y_j \equiv a_j \cdot 1$. So $x \equiv a_j \pmod{m_j}$ for every $j$.

Uniqueness. If $x$ and $x'$ are solutions, each $m_i$ divides $z = x - x'$. We show by induction on $j$ that $m_1 \cdots m_j \mid z$. For $j = 1$ this is given. If $m_1 \cdots m_{j-1} \mid z$, note that $m_1 \cdots m_{j-1}$ is coprime to $m_j$ (first fact) and $m_j \mid z$, so by the second fact $m_1 \cdots m_j \mid z$. At $j = k$ we get $M \mid x - x'$.

blocks.title: The formula and the structure
blocks.body:
The proof gives a formula. For the Sunzi problem, $M = 105$ and
$$M_1 = 35 \equiv 2 \pmod 3,\ y_1 = 2; \qquad M_2 = 21 \equiv 1 \pmod 5,\ y_2 = 1; \qquad M_3 = 15 \equiv 1 \pmod 7,\ y_3 = 1.$$
Then $$x = 2 \cdot 35 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 21 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 15 \cdot 1 = 233 \equiv 23 \pmod{105}$$. The numbers $M_i y_i$ (here $70, 21, 15$) depend only on the moduli; once computed, they solve the system for any remainders. By hand, however, it is often quicker to substitute one congruence into the next, as in the first example below.

Now the structural version. For coprime $m$ and $n$, consider the map
$$\mathbb Z/mn\mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z, \qquad x \mapsto (x \bmod m,\ x \bmod n).$$
It is well defined (if $mn \mid x - x'$ then $m$ and $n$ divide $x - x'$), and it respects addition and multiplication, done coordinate by coordinate on the right. The theorem says it is a bijection. So, as rings,
$$\mathbb Z/mn\mathbb Z \;\cong\; \mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z \quad (\gcd(m,n)=1).$$
Any question about arithmetic modulo $mn$ splits into the same question modulo $m$ and modulo $n$. For example, $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$ means $x \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 3$ and $x \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 5$: $2 \times 2 = 4$ combinations, giving the solutions $1, 4, 11, 14$. Similarly, $x$ is a unit modulo $mn$ exactly when its two coordinates are units, so the number of units is multiplicative: $\varphi(mn) = \varphi(m)\varphi(n)$ for coprime $m, n$, where $\varphi$ counts units (see [[arithmetic-functions]]).

blocks.title: When the moduli share a factor
blocks.body:
If the moduli are not coprime, a solution may or may not exist. For two congruences $x \equiv a \pmod m$ and $x \equiv b \pmod n$ with $g = \gcd(m, n)$:

The system is solvable if and only if $g \mid a - b$, and then the solution is unique modulo $\operatorname{lcm}(m, n)$.

Proof: the first congruence means $x = a + mt$. The second becomes $mt \equiv b - a \pmod n$, a linear congruence in $t$, solvable exactly when $g \mid b - a$ ([[mod-inverse]]). Its solutions form one class $t \equiv t_0$ modulo $n/g$, so $x = a + mt$ is determined modulo $m \cdot \frac{n}{g} = \operatorname{lcm}(m, n)$.

For instance $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $x \equiv 3 \pmod 6$ is solvable since $2 \mid 2$, with $x \equiv 9 \pmod{12}$; but $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $x \equiv 2 \pmod 6$ is not, since the first makes $x$ odd and the second even.

blocks.title: Successive substitution
blocks.solution:
The moduli are pairwise coprime, so there is a unique solution modulo $180$. Substitute step by step. From the second congruence $x = 4 + 5s$. Then $4 + 5s \equiv s \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, so $s = 3 + 4u$ and $x = 19 + 20u$.

Now impose the third: $19 + 20u \equiv 1 + 2u \equiv 1 \pmod 9$, so $2u \equiv 0 \pmod 9$, and since $2$ is invertible modulo $9$, $u \equiv 0 \pmod 9$. Hence
$$x \equiv 19 \pmod{180}.$$
Check: $19 = 4 \cdot 4 + 3 = 3 \cdot 5 + 4 = 2 \cdot 9 + 1$.

blocks.title: Numbers that reproduce their last digits
blocks.body: Find all $x$ with $0 \le x < 1000$ such that $x^2$ ends in the same three digits as $x$, i.e. $x^2 \equiv x \pmod{1000}$.
blocks.solution:
The condition is $1000 \mid x(x-1)$, and $1000 = 8 \cdot 125$ with $\gcd(8, 125) = 1$. Consecutive integers $x$ and $x - 1$ are coprime, so one of them is odd, and $8$ must divide the other one. Likewise at most one of them is divisible by $5$, so all three factors of $5$ in $x(x-1)$ come from that one, and $125$ divides it. Hence the condition is
$$x \equiv 0 \text{ or } 1 \pmod 8 \quad \text{and} \quad x \equiv 0 \text{ or } 1 \pmod{125}.$$
By the CRT each of the four combinations gives exactly one $x$ modulo $1000$. Two are obvious: $(0, 0)$ gives $0$ and $(1, 1)$ gives $1$.

For $x \equiv 1 \pmod{125}$, $x \equiv 0 \pmod 8$: write $x = 1 + 125k$. Since $125 \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, we need $1 + 5k \equiv 0$, i.e. $5k \equiv 7 \pmod 8$. The inverse of $5$ modulo $8$ is $5$, so $k \equiv 35 \equiv 3$, and $x = 376$.

For $x \equiv 0 \pmod{125}$, $x \equiv 1 \pmod 8$: $x = 125k$ with $5k \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, so $k \equiv 5$ and $x = 625$.

The answers are $0, 1, 376, 625$. Indeed $376^2 = 141376$ and $625^2 = 390625$. Notice $376 + 625 = 1001 \equiv 1$: in coordinates these two are $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$, and they add to $(1, 1)$.

blocks.title: Runs of non-squarefree numbers
blocks.body: Show that for every $k$ there are $k$ consecutive positive integers each divisible by a perfect square greater than $1$. For $k = 3$, find the smallest positive $x$ with $4 \mid x$, $9 \mid x + 1$ and $25 \mid x + 2$.
blocks.solution:
Take distinct primes $p_1, \dots, p_k$. The squares $p_1^2, \dots, p_k^2$ are pairwise coprime, so by the CRT there is a positive $x$ with
$$x \equiv -i \pmod{p_{i+1}^2} \qquad (i = 0, 1, \dots, k-1).$$
Then $p_{i+1}^2 \mid x + i$ for each $i$, so $x, x+1, \dots, x+k-1$ all work.

For $k = 3$ with $4, 9, 25$ we need $x \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, $x \equiv -1 \equiv 8 \pmod 9$, $x \equiv -2 \equiv 23 \pmod{25}$. From $x = 4s$ and $4s \equiv 8 \pmod 9$ we get $s \equiv 2$ (cancel the unit $4$), so $x \equiv 8 \pmod{36}$. Then $x = 8 + 36t$ with $8 + 36t \equiv 8 + 11t \equiv 23 \pmod{25}$, so $11t \equiv 15$. Since $11 \cdot 16 = 176 \equiv 1 \pmod{25}$, $t \equiv 15 \cdot 16 = 240 \equiv 15$, and $x = 8 + 36 \cdot 15 = 548$.

So $548 = 4 \cdot 137$, $549 = 9 \cdot 61$, $550 = 25 \cdot 22$, and the general solution is $548 + 900n$. (The order in which the squares are assigned matters: $124 = 4 \cdot 31$, $125 = 25 \cdot 5$, $126 = 9 \cdot 14$ is the smallest triple that uses $4, 9, 25$ in some order, and with other squares allowed the smallest triple is $48 = 16 \cdot 3$, $49 = 7^2$, $50 = 25 \cdot 2$. The CRT gives existence, not minimality.)

blocks.body:
- The theorem needs pairwise coprimality, not just that all the moduli together have gcd $1$. For $6, 10, 15$ the overall gcd is $1$, but $x \equiv 0 \pmod 6$ and $x \equiv 1 \pmod{10}$ already conflict (parity).
- For non-coprime moduli the answer is unique modulo the lcm, not the product: $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $x \equiv 3 \pmod 6$ gives $x \equiv 9 \pmod{12}$, not modulo $24$.
- The formula $\sum a_i M_i y_i$ usually produces a large number; reduce it modulo $M$ at the end.
- The $y_i$ are inverses of $M_i$ modulo $m_i$, not modulo $M$.

The CRT is how one studies a modulus one prime power at a time. It reduces solving a polynomial congruence modulo $n$ to solving it modulo the prime powers dividing $n$, and [[hensel]] then often reduces each prime power to the prime itself. The multiplicativity of $\varphi$ in [[arithmetic-functions]] is a direct consequence, as shown above, and [[dirichlet-characters]] modulo $n$ are built from characters modulo the prime powers of $n$. [[covering-systems]] are families of congruences that together cover every integer, and the CRT is the basic tool for checking whether a given family does.

In [[rsa]], decryption modulo $n = pq$ is typically done modulo $p$ and modulo $q$ separately and recombined with the CRT, which is several times faster. Residue number systems represent big integers by their residues modulo several small coprime numbers, so that addition and multiplication can be done in parallel. Threshold secret-sharing schemes such as those of Mignotte and Asmuth–Bloom use the integer CRT directly; Shamir's scheme uses Lagrange interpolation, which is the same theorem for polynomials, with the pairwise coprime moduli $x - x_1, \dots, x - x_k$.

In algebra the theorem holds for any pairwise coprime [[ideals]] of a commutative ring, where $I$ and $J$ count as coprime when $I + J$ is the whole ring.

1. Solve $x \equiv 2 \pmod 5$, $x \equiv 3 \pmod 7$, $x \equiv 4 \pmod 9$.
2. Is the system $x \equiv 5 \pmod{12}$, $x \equiv 11 \pmod{18}$ solvable? If so, modulo what is the solution unique?
3. How many solutions does $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{1001}$ have? ($1001 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13$.)
4. Show that there are four consecutive positive integers each divisible by a perfect cube greater than $1$.
